attributes.title: AI use and responsible delivery policy
attributes.description: AI use and responsible delivery policy
attributes.markdown:
# Course AI agreement

A proposed teaching policy; the instructor sets the local rules before delivery.

1. Start every task with your own interpretation, design or failing test; then you may ask an assistant for gaps, counterexamples or a review.
2. Use synthetic data only: no real names, e-mail addresses, credentials or private repositories in a prompt.
3. Before accepting a suggestion, inspect it, run the relevant tests and record accept, modify or reject with the reason.
4. Distinguish a command you ran, with its observed output, from a claim an assistant made.
5. Attribute reused code and generated text; check the licence before redistribution.
6. Working without AI is always possible: a peer or the instructor provides the same critique.
7. AI feedback is advisory. The instructor assesses the actual work; no generated response establishes competence.

attributes.title: TaskBoard project brief
attributes.description: TaskBoard project brief
attributes.markdown:
# TaskBoard

Teams of two build TaskBoard, a small task-sharing service for a study group, with synthetic data only. A member creates a task with a title,
an owner and a deadline; shares it with other members; marks it done; and receives a reminder the day before the deadline. The service has an
HTTP or command-line interface of the team's choice, an in-memory store and automated tests. Four milestones follow the modules: requirements
(M1), design (M2), verified deadline reminders (M3) and a reviewed, documented release (M4). Every milestone includes an AI-use note: what was
asked, what was accepted, modified or rejected, and the evidence for the decision.

      "key": "reasoning",

        "The choices cannot be explained.",

      ]

      "key": "judgment",
      "weight": 30,
      "descriptors": [
        "An AI or peer suggestion is accepted without inspection.",
        "A suggestion is recorded but the decision lacks evidence.",

        "The note also states the remaining uncertainty and a no-AI check."
      ]

attributes.title: M1: Requirements with AI critique
attributes.description: M1: Requirements with AI critique
attributes.markdown:
# M1: Requirements with AI critique

## Outcome
Write user stories with testable acceptance criteria for TaskBoard and use an assistant only to find gaps.

## Case
A product owner sends a vague request: 'students need to share tasks and see deadlines'. An assistant drafts ten stories, two of which invent a payment feature and store real e-mail addresses.

## Task
Write five user stories in the INVEST style with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and a list of open questions; ask an assistant for missing edge cases using synthetic data only.

## Checks
Every story has at least one negative acceptance criterion; no story contains invented features or personal data; every open question names who must answer it.

## Weak suggestion to challenge
The generated stories add a feature nobody asked for and an untestable criterion ('the app is fast').

## Submission
Story map, acceptance criteria, open-question list and AI-use note. Answer individually: Which generated story did you reject or rewrite, and what evidence from the request justified it?

attributes.title: M2: Design and modelling decisions
attributes.description: M2: Design and modelling decisions
attributes.markdown:
# M2: Design and modelling decisions

## Outcome
Design the TaskBoard components and justify one design decision against an AI-proposed alternative.

## Case
An assistant proposes a single TaskManager class that parses requests, stores tasks, sends notifications and formats output.

## Task
Draw a component and class diagram for three stories of M1; assign responsibilities; compare your design with the assistant's god-class proposal on cohesion, coupling and testability.

## Checks
Each story is traceable to the components it uses; no component owns two unrelated reasons to change; the decision record names one rejected alternative and its cost.

## Weak suggestion to challenge
The proposed god class makes every change touch the same file and cannot be tested without the notification service.

## Submission
Component diagram, class responsibilities table and architecture decision record. Answer individually: Which responsibility did you move out of the proposed class, and how does a test show the benefit?

attributes.title: M3: Testing AI-generated code
attributes.description: M3: Testing AI-generated code
attributes.markdown:
# M3: Testing AI-generated code

## Outcome
Verify an AI-generated implementation with requirement-derived tests and decide whether to accept it.

## Case
An assistant generates the deadline-reminder function and its tests; all tests pass, but they only repeat the implementation's arithmetic.

## Task
Derive boundary tests from the acceptance criteria (deadline today, tomorrow, past, time zones); run them against the generated code; record which tests fail and fix or reject the code.

## Checks
At least one test fails on the generated code before the fix; tests use a fixed clock; the record separates commands run from claims.

## Weak suggestion to challenge
The generated tests assert the same off-by-one computation as the code and therefore cannot detect it.

## Submission
Test suite, execution trace, defect note and accept/reject decision. Answer individually: What did the passing generated tests fail to prove, and which human-written test exposed it?

attributes.title: M4: Code review, maintenance and responsible delivery
attributes.description: M4: Code review, maintenance and responsible delivery
attributes.markdown:
# M4: Code review, maintenance and responsible delivery

## Outcome
Review and refactor a teammate's change, with AI as one reviewer, and deliver a documented, reproducible release.

## Case
A pull request mixes a refactoring with a behaviour change and includes a code snippet copied from an assistant without attribution.

## Task
Split the pull request into focused commits; review it with a checklist; ask an assistant for a second review and compare it with a peer's; write the release notes and the data/attribution statement.

## Checks
Behaviour is unchanged by the refactoring commit (tests show it); every review comment is addressed or answered; the release states its data handling and the origin of reused code.

## Weak suggestion to challenge
The AI review approves the change and suggests renaming variables but misses the behaviour change hidden in the refactoring.

## Submission
Focused commits, review record, release notes and responsible-delivery statement. Answer individually: Which issue did the human review find that the AI review missed, and how will the team check it next time?

attributes.challenge: Students engineer a small service from requirements to release while using AI assistants critically, showing testable requirements, justified design, executed verification and responsible delivery.

attributes.knowledge: Second-year computer science students who can program in one language and have used version control.
attributes.attitude: Some overtrust generated code, others avoid AI; both practise evidence-based judgment.
attributes.confidence: Mixed; paired work, instructor modelling and individual teach-backs build independence.

attributes.description: Specify, design, verify and deliver TaskBoard, a small task-sharing service, using AI as a fallible collaborator under human verification.

attributes.markdown:
# Course AI agreement

A proposed teaching policy; the instructor sets the local rules before delivery.

1. Start every task with your own interpretation, design or failing test; then you may ask an assistant for gaps, counterexamples or a review.
2. Use synthetic data only: no real names, e-mail addresses, credentials or private repositories in a prompt.
3. Before accepting a suggestion, inspect it, run the relevant tests and record accept, modify or reject with the reason.
4. Distinguish a command you ran, with its observed output, from a claim an assistant made.
5. Attribute reused code and generated text; check the licence before redistribution.
6. Working without AI is always possible: a peer or the instructor provides the same critique.
7. AI feedback is advisory. The instructor assesses the actual work; no generated response establishes competence.

attributes.markdown:
# M1: Requirements with AI critique

## Outcome
Write user stories with testable acceptance criteria for TaskBoard and use an assistant only to find gaps.

## Case
A product owner sends a vague request: 'students need to share tasks and see deadlines'. An assistant drafts ten stories, two of which invent a payment feature and store real e-mail addresses.

## Task
Write five user stories in the INVEST style with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and a list of open questions; ask an assistant for missing edge cases using synthetic data only.

## Checks
Every story has at least one negative acceptance criterion; no story contains invented features or personal data; every open question names who must answer it.

## Weak suggestion to challenge
The generated stories add a feature nobody asked for and an untestable criterion ('the app is fast').

## Submission
Story map, acceptance criteria, open-question list and AI-use note. Answer individually: Which generated story did you reject or rewrite, and what evidence from the request justified it?

attributes.markdown:
# M4: Code review, maintenance and responsible delivery

## Outcome
Review and refactor a teammate's change, with AI as one reviewer, and deliver a documented, reproducible release.

## Case
A pull request mixes a refactoring with a behaviour change and includes a code snippet copied from an assistant without attribution.

## Task
Split the pull request into focused commits; review it with a checklist; ask an assistant for a second review and compare it with a peer's; write the release notes and the data/attribution statement.

## Checks
Behaviour is unchanged by the refactoring commit (tests show it); every review comment is addressed or answered; the release states its data handling and the origin of reused code.

## Weak suggestion to challenge
The AI review approves the change and suggests renaming variables but misses the behaviour change hidden in the refactoring.

## Submission
Focused commits, review record, release notes and responsible-delivery statement. Answer individually: Which issue did the human review find that the AI review missed, and how will the team check it next time?

# M2: Design and modelling decisions

## Outcome
Design the TaskBoard components and justify one design decision against an AI-proposed alternative.

## Case
An assistant proposes a single TaskManager class that parses requests, stores tasks, sends notifications and formats output.

## Task
Draw a component and class diagram for three stories of M1; assign responsibilities; compare your design with the assistant's god-class proposal on cohesion, coupling and testability.

## Checks
Each story is traceable to the components it uses; no component owns two unrelated reasons to change; the decision record names one rejected alternative and its cost.

## Weak suggestion to challenge
The proposed god class makes every change touch the same file and cannot be tested without the notification service.

## Submission
Component diagram, class responsibilities table and architecture decision record. Answer individually: Which responsibility did you move out of the proposed class, and how does a test show the benefit?
